b: The fun of puzzle-box shows rarely lies in arriving at the (often underwhelming) answers to their most pressing mysteries. Rather, it’s in beholding how the characters respond to their slowly escalating circumstances—and each other. In the fourth and final season of Yellowjackets, Ashley Lyle and Bart Nickerson’s epic survival drama about teens stranded in the wilderness, the real treasure has always been the friends they ate along the way.

The final season does serve its ravenous fans a few explanations, but in the eight episodes made available to critics, these prove to be the least satisfying part. By augmenting its narrative structure while both tightening and playfully exploding its central relationships, Yellowjackets emerges as a return to form, and a messy, riveting conclusion to a messy, riveting series.

Last season’s finale answered one long-gestating question by identifying the “pit girl” (that is, the Yellowjackets striker hunted, skewered, and devoured by her savage teammates) first teased in the show’s opening scene. It also left viewers with an equally spiky cliffhanger: With a stolen satellite phone, Natalie (Sophie Thatcher) was able to contact the outside world, a rescue operation was imminent, and we’d soon finally learn how the girls got back home.

Well, soon-ish. The season’s first episode, cheekily titled “Hivemind,” situates us in not the usual two but three separate timelines: the present, in which Misty (Christina Ricci) and Taissa (Tawny Cypress) scheme to bump off the increasingly unhinged Shauna (Melanie Lynskey) while Melissa (Hilary Swank) takes a dangerous, hair-brained gamble on safeguarding her family; the final harrowing days leading up to the teens’ rescue in the wilderness, in which a quick headcount informs us that not everyone is making it out alive; and the immediate aftermath of their rescue, which sees the surviving Yellowjackets attempt to reacclimate to their humdrum lives while ensuring no one squeals on what they got up to in the forest.

The new timeline not only sheds light on some gaps—like how teenage Misty’s (Samantha Hanratty) penchant for ethically dubious detective work gets developed or how Taissa (Jasmin Savoy Brown) and Van’s (Liv Hewson) young romance disintegrates—but it also works to further deepen the show’s central theme of trauma’s long-tail effects. The girls are in turn coddled, bullied, and alienated by their families and peers upon their return, and even after splintering apart and trying to settle back into old routines, the bonds formed by their shared experience keep pulling them back together, for better and worse.

This wrinkle in the established formula can be disorienting at first, as we’ve become so used to watching the characters scavenge and stab each other in the back (literally and figuratively) in the Canadian Rockies that seeing them in fluorescent-bulbed classrooms and keggers can feel staid. Certain plotlines satisfyingly carry diegetic and emotional significance in the present, such as how the reconciliation between short-fused teenage Shauna (Sophie Nélisse) and doofy Jeff (Samuel Braun) after their reunion informs their divorce proceedings. An episode focused largely on Natalie’s stint volunteering as an EMT adds some texture to her character’s tragic (already concluded) arc, but it ultimately provides no forward momentum to later affairs.

Then again, how much does something as conventional as “forward momentum” really matter in a series about the ways in which both time and broken people don’t progress as much as they regress, revert, and circle the drain? When “Hivemind” drops us off in a Canadian hospital with the newly rescued teens, it’s clear from Shauna’s bruised face and Lottie’s (Courtney Eaton) sullen expression that everything that occurred in the woods suspended these characters in a state of aggrieved stasis, where making it out alive doesn’t necessarily mean making it out. After a skeptical chief investigator (Alessandro Juliani) suggests the teens, who all share the same canned word-for-word story of their time in the woods, aren’t acting normal, the hospital’s resident trauma counselor (Cynthia Stevenson) responds in a way that could sum up the entire show’s ethos: “I don’t think there’s a normal in a situation like this.”

The promise of Yellowjackets has always been that it exists as multiple shows operating at once. Is it a coming-of-age soap opera? A psychological-supernatural thriller? A meta black comedy about suburban ennui and the feminist dream deferred? It’s all and yet none of these: Much like the hungry, petty footballers stranded in the woods, the genres cannibalize each other, allowing Yellowjackets to coagulate into a finely tuned, oddball series that’s most gripping when it defies common practice and its characters defy common decency.

That much, in its final season, hasn’t changed—a scene involving an axe, a fire poker, and a pregnant teen is a riot—nor have its sumptuous formal elements. As always, the show’s chilly atmosphere and arch tone flourish thanks to the clever cinematography (the dire wilderness timeline is all muted whites and blacks, while the dreary present is all burnt oranges and piss-yellows), the killer soundtrack (Sublime’s “Santeria” fittingly opens the season, its blue-beat reggae style a gossamer coating that barely hides a tale of murder and violence against women), and the uniformly excellent performances from the actors.

Yellowjackets remains as addictive a show as you’ll find in 2026. While my guess is as good as anyone’s as to how things will wrap up, it’s unlikely we’ll get either a they-were-dead-the-whole-time twist or a laundry list of answers to the show’s lingering mysteries. The only thing that’s certain is that it will be bloody, heartbreaking, and bonkers.

Cast: Melanie Lynskey, Christina Ricci, Tawny Cypress, Sophie Nélisse, Jasmin Savoy Brown, Sophie Thatcher, Samantha Hanratty, Courtney Eaton, Liv Hewson, Warren Kole, Kevin Alves, Sarah Desjardins, Jenna Burgess, Hilary Swank, Molly Ringwald, June Squibb Network: Paramount+
